what: Trinity, the first nuclear test (New Mexico): recording instruments were paralyzed by pickup at the moment of the explosion despite double shielding of signal lines; the effect was later attributed to the nuclear EMP.

sources.title: Nuclear electromagnetic pulse
sources.quote: In spite of this many records were lost because of spurious pickup at the time of the explosion that paralyzed the recording equipment.

sources.title: Nuclear electromagnetic pulse
sources.quote: During the first United States nuclear test on 16 July 1945, electronic equipment was shielded because Enrico Fermi expected the electromagnetic pulse.

note: The quoted technical-history line is quoted via Wikipedia, not read in the original report. Considered later events: British 1952-53 tests ('radioflash' instrument failures), Hardtack Yucca 1958 (first openly reported high-altitude EMP observation), Starfish Prime 1962 (damage to civilian electronics in Hawaii, the first pass choice). Starfish Prime is the first damage to ordinary electrical equipment and first public awareness, but Trinity is the earliest case of electronic equipment disabled by nuclear EMP. Attribution of the 1945 losses to EMP is retrospective, hence medium. Hardening: the 1945 shielding was an early precaution; no distinct first_practical_use or mass_adoption event sourced.

what: Bell Labs' Audrey, built by Balashek, Biddulph and Davis, recognized spoken digits from a single speaker.

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1952 – Bell Labs researchers, Stephen Balashek, R. Biddulph, and K. H. Davis, built Audrey for single-speaker digit recognition.

sources.title: speech recognition (Q189436)
sources.quote: start time (P580): 1952

note: Earlier candidate: Radio Rex (Elmwood Button Co., 1922), a toy dog that leaps out of its house when its name is called. Rejected: it is triggered by acoustic energy near 500 Hz (the vowel in 'Rex'), not by recognizing words, so it is a sound-triggered switch; I also could not fetch a source page for it. Other candidates: RCA 1956 Olson-Belar syllable recognizer, IBM Shoebox 1962 (16 words), all later. Voice-operated doors/locks: no earlier working example found.

what: The Apricot Portable shipped with voice-command recognition (up to 4096 words, 64 in RAM at a time).

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1984 – the Apricot Portable was released with up to 4096 words support, of which only 64 could be held in RAM at a time.

note: Wikipedia lists the Apricot Portable first under 'Practical products'. Earlier commercial use likely exists: Threshold Technology's VIP-100 (about 1972, used for factory quality-control data entry), reported by secondary sources I could not fetch. Reject 1987 Kurzweil and 1990 DragonDictate as later. Treat 1984 as an upper bound; true first use is probably early 1970s.

what: Apple launched the iPhone 4S with Siri, putting spoken commands in the hands of ordinary phone users.

sources.title: Siri
sources.quote: On October 14, 2011, Apple launched the iPhone 4S with a beta version of Siri.

note: The first pass gave 2011-10-04, which is the announcement; the iPhone 4S went on sale 14 October 2011. Earlier but narrower mass uses: telephone call-routing by voice (AT&T 1992), DragonDictate/NaturallySpeaking for PC users (1990s) were niche, not routine for ordinary people.

what: IBM's Tangora, a voice-activated typewriter handling a 20,000-word vocabulary, built by Fred Jelinek's team.

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: By the mid-1980s, Fred Jelinek's team at IBM created a voice-activated typewriter called Tangora, which could handle a 20,000-word vocabulary.

note: Year is only 'mid-1980s' in the source; 1985 is an approximation. Almost certainly too late: RCA's Olson and Belar built an experimental 'phonetic typewriter' that typed from speech and published it in J. Acoust. Soc. Am. in 1956 (found via search; I could not fetch a page to quote, so not used). That earlier prototype, limited to a single talker and a small phoneme set, is the likely true first demonstration.

what: Dragon Dictate released as a consumer dictation product (discrete words, DOS).

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1990 – Dragon Dictate, a consumer product released in 1990.

note: First pass said 1997 NaturallySpeaking, which was the first continuous-speech product, not the first dictation product. The same Wikipedia list gives 1987 'a recognizer from Kurzweil Applied Intelligence' (Kurzweil's medical-report dictation system); the line has no detail, so I could not confirm it as dictation and kept 1990. An earlier 1987 or 1984-85 product may fit. No mass_adoption sourced: dictation by speech only became routine on smartphones in the 2010s, but no fetched source states it.

what: Wolfgang von Kempelen's bellows-operated acoustic-mechanical speech machine, with models of tongue and lips producing vowels and consonants, described in a 1791 paper.

sources.title: Speech synthesis
sources.quote: There followed the bellows-operated "acoustic-mechanical speech machine" of Wolfgang von Kempelen of Pressburg, Hungary, described in a 1791 paper.

sources.title: Wolfgang von Kempelen
sources.quote: Kempelen also created a manually operated speaking machine.

note: Date is the publication of his description; he worked on the machine for about twenty years before, so a working demonstration probably came earlier (the same page gives 1789 for his book, so sources conflict). Earlier candidate: Kratzenstein 1779, vocal-tract models producing five vowels only, rejected as not producing speech. Later: Voder 1939 (first electronic, human-operated, shown at the New York World's Fair), Kelly-Gerstman IBM 7090 computer synthesis 1961, Umeda's English text-to-speech 1968. The machine was hand-operated, as was the Voder.

what: Telesensory Systems' Speech+ talking calculator for the blind, with a synthesized voice, was in use; the Kurzweil Reading Machine for the Blind (Votrax synthesizer) appeared in the same year.

sources.title: Speech synthesis
sources.quote: One of the first was the Telesensory Systems Inc. (TSI) Speech+ portable calculator for the blind in 1976.

note: Earlier systems existed (Umeda's 1968 text-to-speech, MUSA 1975 reading Italian) but I found no evidence they were used outside the lab. Voder (1939) and Kempelen's machine were exhibitions. Date 1976 is the source's year for 'one of the first' handheld devices; a slightly earlier use is possible.

what: Siri on the iPhone 4S brought a talking computer that answers aloud to ordinary phone users.

sources.title: Siri
sources.quote: On October 14, 2011, Apple launched the iPhone 4S with a beta version of Siri.

note: Judgment call. Earlier mass-market talking devices: Texas Instruments Speak & Spell (1978) and talking games and chess computers (1979-80), which had voices but little routine use as 'answering computers'. Wikipedia source supports the date of launch, not the synthesis itself.

what: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA, developed at MIT 1964-67 and first published in 1966, held typed English conversations by pattern matching.

sources.title: Chatbot
sources.quote: Joseph Weizenbaum's program ELIZA was first published in 1966.

sources.title: ELIZA
sources.quote: ELIZA is an early natural language processing computer program developed from 1964 to 1967 at MIT by Joseph Weizenbaum.

note: ELIZA gives the illusion of understanding (the author said so), so the fit to 'understanding questions' is partial; I kept it as the earliest program that held a conversation. Earlier question-answering programs (BASEBALL, 1961; SAD SAM, 1957) answered narrow questions without dialogue and I did not source them. Later: SHRDLU 1970, PARRY 1972. First pass month 1966-01 is not confirmed by a fetched source, so only the year is given.

what: OpenAI released ChatGPT; it reached 100 million users in two months.

sources.title: ChatGPT
sources.quote: ChatGPT gained one million users in five days and 100 million in two months.

note: Earlier mass-market assistants (Siri 2011, Alexa 2014) took commands and short questions rather than holding conversations; chatbots such as SmarterChild (2001) were popular but I did not source them. No first_practical_use is given: no fetched source identifies an out-of-lab deployment before the 1990s and I could not settle it.

what: Georgetown University and IBM translated more than sixty Russian sentences into English automatically on an IBM 701.

sources.title: Georgetown-IBM experiment
sources.quote: The Georgetown–IBM experiment was an influential demonstration of machine translation, which was performed on January 7, 1954.

sources.title: Machine translation
sources.quote: A demonstration was made in 1954 on the APEXC machine at Birkbeck College

note: The 1954 Birkbeck APEXC demonstration (rudimentary English to French; day not given) is the same year and I cannot tell which came first, so the Georgetown date is kept. Mid-1930s patents by Artsrouni (mechanical bilingual dictionary on punched tape) and Troyanskii were proposals or a word-lookup aid, not demonstrated translation. The system was a small demonstration (250 words, six rules).

what: IBM's Automatic Language Translator (AN/GSQ-16) was installed at the US Air Force Foreign Technology Division to convert Soviet technical documents to English.

sources.title: AN/GSQ-16 Automatic Language Translator
sources.quote: The translator was installed in 1959, dramatically upgraded in 1964, and was eventually replaced by a mainframe running SYSTRAN in 1970.

note: Single Wikipedia source. Another source (a 1997 NAIC paper, found by search, not fetched) says the Mark II system was installed at Wright-Patterson in 1964 as one of the first operational MT systems, so the 1959 installation may have been a pre-operational version. Other early uses I did not verify: Georgetown/Euratom/Atomic Energy Commission systems in the early 1960s; METEO weather-bulletin translation (1970s).

what: AltaVista Babel Fish (SYSTRAN) offered free web translation to the public and handled about 500,000 requests a day.

sources.title: Machine translation
sources.quote: AltaVista Babelfish, which racked up 500,000 requests a day (1997)

note: First free web translation was SYSTRAN's 1996 offering; 1997 is when it reached large daily use. Google Translate (April 2006) later brought it to hundreds of millions. 'Routine' use by ordinary people is arguable for 1997; a later date (2006) could also be argued.

what: Marian Rejewski's 'bomba kryptologiczna', an electrically driven aggregate of six Enigma machines at the Polish Cipher Bureau, designed about October 1938 and ready in mid-November 1938.

sources.title: Bomba (cryptography)
sources.quote: In mid-November 1938, the bombs were ready, and the reconstructing of daily keys now took about two hours.

sources.title: Bomba (cryptography)
sources.quote: invented the "bomba kryptologiczna" (cryptologic bomb), probably in October 1938

note: Earlier candidate: the Polish cyclometer (designed 'probably in 1934 or 1935'), which catalogued cycle structures of Enigma permutations to speed decryption. Rejected as the first because it prepared a catalogue rather than testing keys itself, though it arguably also fits 'analysing patterns'. The British Bombe (1940), Heath Robinson (1943) and Colossus (Mark 1 first attacked a message on 5 February 1944) are later; the first pass named Colossus. Before 1938 the Poles used hand 'grill' methods. Pre-electromechanical cryptanalytic machines (e.g. punched-card tabulator aids in the 1930s) were not checked.

what: The Polish bombs were put to use reconstructing the daily Enigma keys at the Cipher Bureau from mid-November 1938.

sources.title: Bomba (cryptography)
sources.quote: In mid-November 1938, the bombs were ready, and the reconstructing of daily keys now took about two hours.

note: Same event as the demonstration: the machines were built for real traffic and operated at the Cipher Bureau, and the source says six were built before September 1939. The page does not quote messages broken on a given day, so 'practical use' rests on the stated purpose. Later pure-practical dates: British Bombe 1940, Colossus 1944.

what: John Clark's Eureka, a mechanical machine that generated Latin hexameter verses automatically (about one a minute), was exhibited at the Egyptian Hall, London, after being built 1830-1845.

sources.title: The Eureka
sources.quote: named John Clark, who then exhibited his invention in the Egyptian Hall in London.

note: Mechanical, not a computer; it fits 'composes poems automatically' but a strict reading of 'a computer' would give Christopher Strachey's love-letter generator on the Ferranti Mark 1 / Manchester Mark 1 (1952), the first computer-generated literature, which is the first pass candidate (the first pass said 1953; sources give summer 1952, one gives 1953). Eureka's method was the published 1677 scheme of John Peter, but Clark fully automated it. Build dates: 1830-1843 (some sources) or 1845. Shannon's 1948 Markov text examples were hand-made and not considered.

what: Environment Canada deployed FoG, which generated weather forecasts in English and French from data automatically.

sources.title: Natural-language generation
sources.quote: The earliest such system to be deployed was FoG, which was used by Environment Canada to generate weather forecasts

note: Source says only 'early 1990s'; 1990 is a placeholder year. Literature I recall gives about 1992 but I did not source it. Later: Reuters Tracer and the Associated Press / Los Angeles Times Quakebot (2014). Earlier practical text generation (e.g. form-letter mail merge) is a template fill, not composition. Eureka (1845) was a paid exhibition, not a practical tool.

what: ChatGPT made automatic writing of text available to ordinary users, reaching 100 million users in two months.

sources.title: ChatGPT
sources.quote: ChatGPT gained one million users in five days and 100 million in two months.

note: Earlier mass exposure was to machine-written news snippets (AP earnings and sports reports since 2014) that readers did not choose or operate; ChatGPT is when ordinary people used machine writing routinely themselves.

what: CSIRAC, Australia's first computer (Trevor Pearcey and Maston Beard, CSIRO, Sydney), was programmed to play music, the first known use of a digital computer for the purpose.

sources.title: CSIRAC
sources.quote: In 1950 CSIRAC was used to play music, the first known use of a digital computer for the purpose.

sources.title: Computer music
sources.quote: The world's first computer to play music was the CSIR Mark 1

note: Fits 'performs music' (playing popular melodies programmed by Geoff Hill) but the music was not composed by the machine. Strachey's Ferranti Mark 1 national anthem in late 1951 is later (first recording). Composition by computer: Illiac Suite (1957; Hiller and Isaacson), 'generally agreed to be the first score composed by an electronic computer', so 'composes' dates to 1956-57. Art: Desmond Paul Henry's drawing machine (1961, adapted analogue bombsight computer), Michael Noll 1962, AARON (from 1972); Ben Laposky's 1950 analogue 'oscillons' were not checked. Earlier automata (Jaquet-Droz 1770s, al-Jazari) replay fixed mechanisms and I excluded them. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption given: the sources found do not mark out a use outside the lab, and AI image generators of 2022 are described only as approaching human quality, not adoption.

what: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds built SNARC at Princeton (funding summer 1951), a neural-net machine that learned by reinforcement to solve a maze.

sources.title: Stochastic neural analog reinforcement calculator
sources.quote: They tested the machine on a copy of Shannon's maze, and found that it could learn to solve the maze.

note: Candidates: Ashby's Homeostat (1948, adapts to disturbances; closer to self-regulation than learning from experience), Shannon's Theseus maze mouse (1950; relays remember the maze path, and whether it 'learned' is disputed), Samuel's checkers program (begun 1949, first ran 1952, paper 1959; 'machine learning' coined 1959) and Rosenblatt's perceptron (1957-58). SNARC is a simulated maze solved by reinforced weights, so I take it as the earliest clear case, but this is a judgment and the date is only the year. Page for Theseus could not be fetched. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption given: ADALINE (1960) adaptive filters and later uses were not sourced, and 'routine' consumer use is too diffuse to date.

what: The first programs that could play a full game of standard chess were written, by Alex Bernstein (IBM 704) and by Russian programmers on a BESM.

sources.title: Computer chess
sources.quote: The first programs that can play a full game of chess are developed, one by Alex Bernstein and one by Russian programmers

note: Earlier candidates and why rejected: El Ajedrecista (Torres Quevedo, 1912), an electromechanical machine playing only king and rook against king (not a program or computer); Turing's Turochamp (1948-52), never run on a computer, played by hand in 1952; Prinz's 1951 Ferranti Mark 1 program, which only solved mate-in-two problems; Los Alamos chess on MANIAC I (1956), the first chess-like game played by a computer program but on a 6x6 board without bishops, a variant, not chess. If the variant counts, 1956 is the answer. Strict reading used here.

what: Fidelity Electronics released Chess Challenger, the first dedicated chess computer sold to the public.

sources.title: Computer chess
sources.quote: In March, Fidelity Electronics releases Chess Challenger, the first dedicated chess computer to be sold.

note: Practical use taken as sale to people who play chess with it. Chess programs ran in the ACM computer chess championships from 1970, but that is competition between programs, not a product. Superhuman level (Deep Blue beating Kasparov, 1997) is not a listed kind. No mass_adoption date is sourced.

what: Westinghouse's Nimatron, an electromechanical relay machine conceived by Edward Condon, played Nim against fairgoers at the New York World's Fair.

sources.title: Nimatron
sources.quote: It was first exhibited in April–October 1940 by the Westinghouse Electric Corporation at the 1939-1940 New York World's Fair to entertain fair-goers.

note: Replaces the first pass's Strachey draughts program (1951-52) and the Nimrod machine (1951), both later. Chess-only machines (El Ajedrecista, 1912) belong to the chess concept. Earlier ideas (Babbage's planned tic-tac-toe automaton, 1840s) were never built. The month is the opening of the 1940 season of the fair; the build was done in the months before.

what: The Nimatron was in public use at the fair as entertainment, with about 100,000 games of Nim played against visitors.

sources.title: Nimatron
sources.quote: The reception of the machine during the fair was positive, with around 100,000 games of Nim played.

note: Same event as the demonstration: the purpose of the machine was to entertain fairgoers, so public exhibition is its real use. No mass_adoption event sourced for game-playing programs as a category.

concept_note: Moved the first demonstration from Starfish Prime (1962) back to Trinity (1945), where recording equipment was paralyzed despite shielding; Starfish Prime is the first damage to civilian electronics. No practical-use or mass-adoption milestone: it is a hazard, and hardening has no distinct sourced first event.

Kept Audrey (1952) as demonstration, rejected Radio Rex (1922) as a sound-triggered switch. Added a practical-use date (1984, low; probably earlier) and corrected the Siri date to 14 Oct 2011 (the first pass date was the announcement). Voice-operated doors not found.

First pass had only NaturallySpeaking 1997, which was a continuous-speech product, not the first. Added IBM Tangora (mid-1980s, low) and DragonDictate 1990; the 1956 RCA phonetic typewriter is probably the real first but could not be sourced. No mass-adoption milestone sourced.

First pass named the 1939 Voder; the earlier Kempelen speaking machine (1791 description) fits the definition and is earlier but weakly dated. Added practical use (1976, low) and mass adoption (Siri 2011, low). Kratzenstein 1779 rejected as vowels only.
Kept ELIZA (1966) with the year only; added ChatGPT as mass adoption (Nov 2022). No first_practical_use found.

Kept Georgetown-IBM (7 Jan 1954), noting the same-year Birkbeck APEXC demonstration. Practical use stays 1959 (low) with a conflicting 1964 Mark II date reported; added Babel Fish 1997 as mass adoption (low).
No milestones. No machine has decoded an unknown language from samples from samples, so there is no demonstration to date.

First pass named Colossus (1944); the Polish bomba (1938) is earlier and breaks Enigma by testing settings, so it replaces it as the demonstration. Cyclometer (c. 1934-35) noted as a catalogue aid. Practical use same date, low. No mass_adoption: not applicable.

First pass had Strachey 1953; found John Clark's Eureka (1845) as an earlier mechanical verse generator, and Strachey is dated summer 1952 by the sources, so the computer-only date is 1952. Added FoG weather forecasts (early 1990s) as practical use and ChatGPT (2022) as mass adoption.

Moved the demonstration from Illiac Suite (1957) to CSIRAC playing music (1950); the Illiac Suite remains the first composition by computer. AARON and other computer art noted but not made milestones. No practical-use or mass-adoption milestone sourced.

Replaced Samuel's 1959 paper with SNARC (1951, low) as the earliest clear learning machine; Theseus (1950), Homeostat (1948), Samuel (1952/1959) and the perceptron considered. No practical-use or mass-adoption milestone sourced.

Demonstration set to 1957 (first full chess games), with Los Alamos 1956 a variant and Turing/Prinz earlier but not playing games on a machine. Added practical use: Chess Challenger, March 1977. No mass-adoption date sourced.
Replaced Strachey's 1951-52 draughts with the Nimatron (1940), a machine that played Nim against the public. Demonstration and practical use are one event. No mass adoption.
No milestones: no machine matches human intelligence across all intellectual tasks, so there is no demonstration to date.
No milestones: no machine is known to be conscious or self-aware; claims have not been established.

_tools: page_text.py worked for Wikipedia (slow, 30-70 s when many run in parallel; run in sequence or few at a time); non-Wikipedia pages (AIP, Semantic Scholar, Hagley, ETHW, Britannica 403) hung or failed, so only Wikipedia and Wikidata sources are used; chronam not used; WebSearch worked for leads (Radio Rex, Olson-Belar, Threshold VIP-100, GSQ-16 1964 date, Theseus) but those could not be quoted. Wikipedia pages for Radio Rex and Theseus (mouse) do not exist or returned empty.
